Electrical Conductivity of Selected Metals at Room Temperature

According to Equation 22.4, the current density flowing through a ma­te­rial sample is proportional to the electric field applied to the sample, and the proportionality constant is the conductivity of the ma­te­rial of which the sample is made. This is the equation we use to relate the conductivity of a ma­te­rial to its microstructural prop- erties. Table 22.6 lists conductivities for several common metals at room temperature.2

Insight into the conductivity is provided by measuring the electrical conductivity of aqueous ionic solutions (Fig. 22.20; this topic is referred to in Chapters 11 and 15). The conductivity of pure water, multiply distilled to remove all impurities, is about 0.043 3 1026 (V cm)21. Exposed to the air, pure water dissolves CO2, which forms carbonic acid, H2CO3; dissociation produces H3O1 and HCO , 3 2 which increase the conductivity to about 1 3 1026 (V cm)21. As ionic solutes are added to water, the conductivity increases rapidly; a 1.0-m solution in NaOH has conductivity of about 0.180 (V cm)21 at 25°C. The conductivity depends strongly on both concentration and ionic species. The concentration dependence is summarized by the ­molar ­conductivity, defined by Lm 5 s/c, where c is the concentration of the ion mea­sured in moles per liter. To gain fundamental understanding of the conduction mechanism, we relate Lm to the details of the ionic motion in dilute solutions in response to the elec- tric field. This leads to the concept of mobility of the ion, denoted by m, which shows how its surroundings influence the response of an ion to an applied field.
